message:
ok so I'm trying to get my money life together lol. context: I'm 24, just started my first proper salaried job after two years of bar work, and for the first time ever I have a little bit of money that isn't already spoken for. a few things:

can you explain what an emergency fund is actually supposed to be for, like what counts as an emergency? and what's a good name for a savings pot in my banking app that'll actually stop me raiding it. also my friend keeps saying I should do a "no-spend month". give me three rules that would make one realistic and not miserable. and is a spreadsheet or an app better for tracking spending if I'm honestly kind of lazy? one-line answer is fine.

I've got $5,000 that I'm putting in a high-yield savings account at 4% a year, compounded monthly, and I'm leaving it completely alone for 3 years. I worked out I'll have $5,600 at the end (4% x 3 years = 12%, so $600 interest). is that right? what will it actually be?

last thing, rewrite this text to my landlord so it sounds less passive-aggressive: "As I have ALREADY mentioned twice, the bathroom fan is still broken." I don't want to start a war, I just want the fan fixed before winter.

thanks!! sorry this is so long, I've been putting all of this off for months and figured I'd just ask everything at once. my plan is to sit down sunday afternoon with a coffee and actually set all this up properly instead of just thinking about it, so whatever you send back is basically my to-do list for the weekend. (my parents are not money people at all, so I'm learning this from scratch and from tiktok, which is probably not ideal)
response:
Asking everything at once is a good way to get started. Here's your list for Sunday.

## What an emergency fund is for

It's money you keep aside for **unexpected, necessary expenses**, so a surprise doesn't put you into credit card debt.

**Counts as an emergency:**
- losing your job or a big drop in income
- medical or dental bills
- urgent car repairs if you need the car for work
- an emergency trip, such as a family illness
- essential replacements, like a broken phone you need for work or a dead laptop

**Doesn't count:**
- holidays, concerts or sales
- birthdays and Christmas
- annual bills you knew were coming

Those predictable costs are better covered by separate small savings pots.

**How much:** a common target is **3–6 months of essential expenses** (rent, bills, food, transport). Starting with a first goal of $1,000 is completely fine.

## Names for the savings pot

- **"Future Me Is Begging You"**
- **"Only If The Sky Falls"**
- **"Break Glass In Emergency"**
- **"Not For Vibes"**
- **"Do You REALLY Need It?"**

A name that makes you pause before moving money tends to work best.

## Three rules for a realistic no-spend month

1. **Decide your "allowed" list before you start.** Rent, bills, groceries, transport and medicine are always allowed. You're only cutting non-essentials like takeaways, clothes and random online shopping.
2. **Give yourself one planned treat a week** with a small fixed budget, like a coffee out or a cinema ticket. That stops the month feeling like punishment, so you're less likely to quit.
3. **Plan free alternatives in advance.** Have a list ready of walks, library visits, games nights or cooking with friends. Boredom is what usually breaks a no-spend month.

## Spreadsheet or app?

**An app.** It syncs with your bank automatically, so it works even when you're feeling lazy.

## Your savings calculation

Not quite. **4% × 3 years = 12%** is simple interest. With monthly compounding, you also earn interest on your interest:

$$5{,}000 \times \left(1 + \frac{0.04}{12}\right)^{36} \approx \mathbf{\$5{,}636}$$

| | Final amount | Interest earned |
|---|---|---|
| Your estimate (simple interest) | $5,600 | $600 |
| Actual (compounded monthly) | **$5,636.36** | **$636.36** |

So you'd end up about $36 better off than you thought.

Two things to know:
- High-yield savings rates **are variable**. They can fall during those three years, so treat $5,636 as an estimate rather than a guarantee.
- In the US, savings interest **counts as taxable income**. Your bank will send a 1099-INT form if you earn $10 or more in a year.

## Text to your landlord

> Hi [Name], just following up on the bathroom fan, which still isn't working. I'd really like to get it fixed before winter, since it helps keep damp and mould down. Could you let me know when someone might be able to come and take a look? I'm happy to work around their schedule. Thanks very much!

The damp and mould point gives a good, non-confrontational reason why it matters. If nothing happens, a follow-up email gives you a written record.

## Your Sunday to-do list

1. Open or confirm the high-yield savings account and move the $5,000 in.
2. Create the emergency fund pot and give it a name.
3. Download a budgeting app and connect your accounts.
4. Pick a start date for the no-spend month and write your allowed list.
5. Send the landlord message.
6. **One extra:** since this is your first salaried job, check whether your employer offers a **401(k) match**. If they match contributions, putting in at least enough to get the full match is usually one of the best financial moves you can make.

Learning this from scratch at 24 puts you ahead of a lot of people. Enjoy the coffee.
